claim: Ntn1 expression in the adult mouse brain is diffuse and low throughout most regions, with moderate expression in the cerebellum and hippocampus, and highest expression in the ventral midbrain (substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area).
source: In situ hybridization analysis of Ntn1 from the Allen Institute mouse brain expression atlas (Lein et al., 2007) shows diffuse and low levels of expression throughout the adult mouse brain, with moderate expression levels in the cerebellum and hippocampus (Figure 1A), and the highest level of expression in the ventral midbrain (substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data from the Allen Institute atlas shown in Figure 1A

claim: Of Ntn1-expressing cells in the VTA, 72.2% co-localize with Th (dopamine neurons) and 18.1% co-localize with Slc32a1 (GABA neurons).
source: Of the identified Ntn1 positive cells, Ntn1 expression co-localized with Th expression (dopamine producing neurons; 72.2% co-localization) and Slc32a1-expressing GABA neurons (18.1% co-localization) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantification from RNAscope in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1E

claim: 64.5% of Th-positive cells in the VTA co-express Ntn1.
source: (F) Of the total of Th+ identified cells, 64.5% co-expressed Ntn1 (35.6% did not express Ntn1), and 30.4% of Slc32a1 identified cells co-expressed Ntn1 (69.5% did not express Ntn1).
evidence: Quantification from RNAscope in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1F

claim: 30.4% of Slc32a1-positive (GABA) cells in the VTA co-express Ntn1.
source: (F) Of the total of Th+ identified cells, 64.5% co-expressed Ntn1 (35.6% did not express Ntn1), and 30.4% of Slc32a1 identified cells co-expressed Ntn1 (69.5% did not express Ntn1).
evidence: Quantification from RNAscope in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1F

claim: Ntn1 protein is present in both Th-positive and Th-negative cells in the VTA.
source: Immunohistochemistry for Ntn1 and Th (Figure 1G) confirmed the presence of Ntn1 in dopamine and non-dopamine producing (Th-negative) cells.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Ntn1 conditional knockout in VTA dopamine neurons results in a significant reduction in the proportion of Th-positive cells co-labeled with Ntn1.
source: Ntn1 conditional knockout (cKO) resulted in a significant reduction in the proportion of VTA Th-positive cells co-labeled with Ntn1 in DAT-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice compared to controls (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 2D-E with statistical significance (p<0.0001)

claim: The average number of Th-positive cells per slice in the VTA was not statistically different between DAT-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice and controls.
source: In contrast to previous findings following Ntn1 deletion in the substantia nigra (Jasmin et al., 2021), the average number of Th + cells per slice was not statistically different in DAT-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice compared to controls (control: 178.2 ± 12.68 and Ntn1 cKO 173.3 ± 10.75).
evidence: Statistical comparison of cell counts between control and Ntn1 cKO groups, with reference to prior work by Jasmin et al., 2021

claim: Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA dopamine neurons results in significantly reduced mEPSC amplitude and frequency.
source: Ntn1 mutagenesis in dopamine neurons resulted in significantly reduced mEPSC amplitude and frequency (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3B-D with statistical significance (p<0.001 for amplitude, p<0.0001 for frequency)

claim: Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA GABA neurons results in significantly reduced mEPSC amplitude and frequency.
source: Similarly, Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA GABA neurons also resulted in significantly reduced mEPSC amplitude and frequency (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F-H with statistical significance (p<0.05 for amplitude, p<0.001 for frequency)

claim: Ntn1 mutagenesis does not significantly affect mIPSCs in VTA dopamine or GABA neurons.
source: We did not detect significant effects on miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) in VTA dopamine or GABA neurons following Ntn1 mutagenesis in these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting Ntn1 does not play a role in regulating inhibitory connectivity in these cells.
evidence: Electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 mutagenesis in either dopamine or GABA neurons does not result in a significant change in paired-pulse ratio.
source: Ntn1 mutagenesis in either dopamine or GABA neurons did not result in a significant change in PPR compared to controls, suggesting no measurable change in presynaptic release (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Paired-pulse ratio electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3J-K with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 mutagenesis in DAT-Cre mice results in significantly reduced AMPA-evoked current in VTA dopamine neurons.
source: Ntn1 mutagenesis in DAT-Cre mice resulted in significantly reduced AMPA-evoked current compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Bath application of AMPA electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D with statistical significance (p=0.008)

claim: NMDA-evoked responses in VTA dopamine neurons are similar between Ntn1 cKO and control mice.
source: In contrast, NMDA-evoked responses were similar between the groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: Bath application of NMDA electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E, F with no statistical significance (p=0.5271)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons does not significantly affect day-night locomotion.
source: First, we monitored day-night locomotion in control and AAV1-FLEX-SaCas9-sgNtn1 injected DAT-Cre mice. No significant differences were detected (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Locomotor activity data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons does not significantly affect FR1 or FR5 operant conditioning performance.
source: We did not observe significant differences in either of these behavioral tasks (Figure 4C).
evidence: Operant conditioning data shown in Figure 4C with no statistical significance for FR1 or FR5

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons does not significantly affect progressive ratio performance.
source: Next, we monitored motivated behavior using a progressive ratio schedule of reinforcement in which the number of lever presses required for reinforcement increases non-arithmetically (1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 19, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61, 73…), and again did not observe significant differences between control and experimental mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Progressive ratio data shown in Figure 4D with no statistical significance (p=0.3525)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons does not significantly affect extinction training.
source: Following PR, we reinstated FR1 responding for three days followed by extinction training, and again did not detect any differences between the two groups (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons did not alter appetitive conditioning behaviors.
evidence: Extinction training data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons results in a slight but significant reduction in body weight prior to calorie restriction.
source: Although appetitive conditioning was not affected by Ntn1 loss of function in dopamine neurons, we did observe a slight but significant reduction in body weight in these mice relative to controls prior to calorie restriction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Body weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance (p<0.05)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons does not significantly affect pre-pulse inhibition percentage.
source: Moreover, we did not observe differences in PPI percentage inhibition (Figure 4G).
evidence: Pre-pulse inhibition data shown in Figure 4G with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons results in increased time on edge and decreased time in center of open field arena, consistent with elevated anxiety-like behavior.
source: AAV1-FLEX-SaCas9-sgNtn1 injected DAT-Cre mice spent significantly more time on the edge of the open field arena and significantly less time in the center of the arena, consistent with an elevation in anxiety-like behavior (Figure 4H).
evidence: Open field test data shown in Figure 4H with statistical significance (p<0.01 for both edge and center)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons results in a significant increase in locomotor activity.
source: In contrast to Ntn1 mutagenesis in dopamine neurons, this manipulation in VTA GABA neurons resulted in a significant increase in locomotor activity (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Locomotor activity data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance (p<0.0001)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons results in increased earned reinforcements in the FR5 schedule.
source: In the FR1 schedule of reinforcement, we did not observe a significant difference between the groups; however, we observed an increase in the number of earned reinforcements in the FR5 schedule in mice with Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: Operant conditioning data shown in Figure 5C with statistical significance for FR5 (p<0.05)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons results in increased breakpoint in the progressive ratio schedule.
source: We also observed an increase in the PR schedule of reinforcement in these mice relative to controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: Progressive ratio data shown in Figure 5D with statistical significance (p<0.05)

claim: Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice display elevated extinction bursts during extinction training compared to controls.
source: However, during extinction training, Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice displayed high extinction bursts (elevated pressing following reward omission) compared to controls that remained elevated on the second day of extinction training (Figure 5E).
evidence: Extinction training data shown in Figure 5E with statistical significance (p<0.01)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons results in a significant reduction in acoustic startle response.
source: Analysis of sensory-motor gating in these mice revealed that Vgat-Cre mice injected with AAV1-FLEX-SaCas9-sgNtn1 had a significant reduction in the acoustic startle relative to control mice (Figure 5F) that was accompanied by a reduction in PPI (Figure 5G).
evidence: Acoustic startle data shown in Figure 5F with statistical significance (p<0.0085)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons results in a reduction in pre-pulse inhibition.
source: Analysis of sensory-motor gating in these mice revealed that Vgat-Cre mice injected with AAV1-FLEX-SaCas9-sgNtn1 had a significant reduction in the acoustic startle relative to control mice (Figure 5F) that was accompanied by a reduction in PPI (Figure 5G).
evidence: Pre-pulse inhibition data shown in Figure 5G with statistical significance (p<0.01)

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA neurons results in increased time on edge in the open field test.
source: Similar to mutagenesis of Ntn1 in dopamine neurons, this manipulation in GABA neurons resulted in an increase in anxiety-like behavior as demonstrated by an increased time on edge; though we only observed a trend towards a reduction in time spent in the center of the open field arena (Figure 5H).
evidence: Open field test data shown in Figure 5H with statistical significance for edge time (p<0.05)

claim: Simultaneous Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA and dopamine neurons largely reverses the hyperlocomotor phenotype observed with Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA GABA neurons alone.
source: Simultaneous Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA and dopamine neurons largely reversed the hyperlocomotor phenotype (Figure 6C) observed with Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA GABA neurons alone, though a modest, increase in daytime locomotion remained (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Locomotor activity data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons results in operant responding during FR1 and FR5 that is similar to controls.
source: Similarly, loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons resulted in operant responding during FR1 and FR5 that was similar to controls (Figure 6D) and pre-calorie restriction body weights did not differ between the groups.
evidence: Operant conditioning data shown in Figure 6D with no statistical significance for FR1 or FR5

claim: Loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons results in elevated motivation in the progressive ratio task.
source: Motivation, as measured in the PR task, was elevated in the double transgenic Cre line following Ntn1 mutagenesis (Figure 6E) and extinction was impaired (Figure 6F), though these phenotypes were less robust than those observed in the VTA GABA-only mice.
evidence: Progressive ratio data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance (p<0.05)

claim: Loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons results in impaired extinction.
source: Motivation, as measured in the PR task, was elevated in the double transgenic Cre line following Ntn1 mutagenesis (Figure 6E) and extinction was impaired (Figure 6F), though these phenotypes were less robust than those observed in the VTA GABA-only mice.
evidence: Extinction data shown in Figure 6F with statistical significance (p<0.05)

claim: Loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons results in acoustic startle and PPI responses similar to control mice.
source: Finally, loss of Ntn1 in both cell types resulted in acoustic startle and PPI responses (Figure 6G–H), and open field activity (Figure 6I) that was similar to control mice.
evidence: Acoustic startle and PPI data shown in Figure 6G-H with no statistical significance

claim: Loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons results in open field activity similar to control mice.
source: Finally, loss of Ntn1 in both cell types resulted in acoustic startle and PPI responses (Figure 6G–H), and open field activity (Figure 6I) that was similar to control mice.
evidence: Open field data shown in Figure 6I with no statistical significance

claim: Proper regulation of the midbrain dopamine system is essential for numerous brain functions and behavior.
source: Proper regulation of the midbrain dopamine system is essential for numerous brain functions and behavior (Bissonette and Roesch, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Bissonette and Roesch, 2016

claim: Disruption in the balance of midbrain dopamine neuron activity has been linked to autism.
source: Disruption in the balance of midbrain dopamine neuron activity has been linked to several neurological and psychiatric conditions, including autism (Pavăl, 2017), schizophrenia (Hietala and Syvälahti, 1996), and substance use disorders (Ostroumov and Dani, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Pavăl, 2017

claim: Disruption in the balance of midbrain dopamine neuron activity has been linked to schizophrenia.
source: Disruption in the balance of midbrain dopamine neuron activity has been linked to several neurological and psychiatric conditions, including autism (Pavăl, 2017), schizophrenia (Hietala and Syvälahti, 1996), and substance use disorders (Ostroumov and Dani, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Hietala and Syvälahti, 1996

claim: Disruption in the balance of midbrain dopamine neuron activity has been linked to substance use disorders.
source: Disruption in the balance of midbrain dopamine neuron activity has been linked to several neurological and psychiatric conditions, including autism (Pavăl, 2017), schizophrenia (Hietala and Syvälahti, 1996), and substance use disorders (Ostroumov and Dani, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Ostroumov and Dani, 2018

claim: Within the VTA, the activity of dopamine neurons is regulated in part by inhibitory (GABAergic) and excitatory (glutamatergic) synaptic input.
source: Within the VTA, the activity of dopamine neurons is regulated in part by inhibitory (GABAergic) and excitatory (glutamatergic) synaptic input.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about VTA circuitry

claim: Genome-wide association studies and analysis of de novo mutations have strongly implicated genes regulating neuronal axon guidance in neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Genome-wide association studies and analysis of de novo mutations have strongly implicated genes regulating neuronal axon guidance in neurodevelopmental disorders (Gilman et al., 2012; Gulsuner et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Gilman et al., 2012 and Gulsuner et al., 2013

claim: The axonal guidance receptor Robo2 is necessary for the maintenance of inhibitory synaptic connectivity in the adult VTA.
source: We previously demonstrated that the axonal guidance receptor Robo2 is necessary for the maintenance of inhibitory synaptic connectivity in the adult VTA (Gore et al., 2017), suggesting that axonal guidance proteins have a critical function in maintaining synaptic connectivity in the adult midbrain.
evidence: Cited from Gore et al., 2017, referring to prior work by the authors

claim: During development, Ntn1 is highly expressed throughout the central nervous system.
source: During development, the gene encoding netrin-1 (Ntn1) is highly expressed throughout the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Ntn1 expression during development

claim: Following the critical developmental period, global Ntn1 expression decreases, but expression within the limbic system, particularly in the ventral midbrain, persists.
source: Following this critical period global expression decreases (Manitt et al., 2010), but expression within the limbic system, particularly in the ventral midbrain, persists.
evidence: Cited from Manitt et al., 2010

claim: Genetic inactivation of Ntn1 from forebrain glutamatergic neurons in late postnatal development results in significantly impaired spatial memory in adult mice.
source: Consistent with the continued function of Ntn1 following early development, genetic inactivation of either Ntn1 (Winberg et al., 1998) or its receptor Dcc Glasgow et al., 2018 from forebrain glutamatergic neurons in late postnatal development results in significantly impaired spatial memory in adult mice that corresponds to a loss of hippocampal plasticity.
evidence: Cited from Winberg et al., 1998 and Glasgow et al., 2018

claim: Genetic inactivation of Dcc from forebrain glutamatergic neurons in late postnatal development results in significantly impaired spatial memory in adult mice that corresponds to a loss of hippocampal plasticity.
source: Consistent with the continued function of Ntn1 following early development, genetic inactivation of either Ntn1 (Winberg et al., 1998) or its receptor Dcc Glasgow et al., 2018 from forebrain glutamatergic neurons in late postnatal development results in significantly impaired spatial memory in adult mice that corresponds to a loss of hippocampal plasticity.
evidence: Cited from Glasgow et al., 2018

claim: Dcc expression levels in adult VTA mice are significantly upregulated following amphetamine exposure.
source: Within the VTA, Dcc expression levels in adult mice are significantly upregulated following amphetamine exposure (Yetnikoff et al., 2010), and Dcc haploinsufficient mice display blunted locomotor response to amphetamine (Flores et al., 2005), consistent with increased excitatory synaptic strength in the VTA following amphetamine treatment (Saal et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Yetnikoff et al., 2010

claim: Dcc haploinsufficient mice display blunted locomotor response to amphetamine.
source: Within the VTA, Dcc expression levels in adult mice are significantly upregulated following amphetamine exposure (Yetnikoff et al., 2010), and Dcc haploinsufficient mice display blunted locomotor response to amphetamine (Flores et al., 2005), consistent with increased excitatory synaptic strength in the VTA following amphetamine treatment (Saal et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Flores et al., 2005

claim: Excitatory synaptic strength in the VTA increases following amphetamine treatment.
source: Within the VTA, Dcc expression levels in adult mice are significantly upregulated following amphetamine exposure (Yetnikoff et al., 2010), and Dcc haploinsufficient mice display blunted locomotor response to amphetamine (Flores et al., 2005), consistent with increased excitatory synaptic strength in the VTA following amphetamine treatment (Saal et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Saal et al., 2003

claim: Ntn1 regulates excitatory synaptic connectivity in the adult hippocampus.
source: Previous research has shown that Ntn1 regulates excitatory synaptic connectivity in the adult hippocampus (Glasgow et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Glasgow et al., 2018

claim: Ntn1 loss of function significantly reduces postsynaptic glutamate receptor-mediated currents in a cell-autonomous manner in the adult hippocampus.
source: We find that Ntn1 loss of function significantly reduces postsynaptic glutamate receptor-mediated currents in a cell-autonomous manner similar to what has been reported previously in the adult hippocampus (Glasgow et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Glasgow et al., 2018 and supported by the current study's electrophysiology data

claim: Ntn1 regulates the delivery of GluA1-containing AMPA receptors to the postsynaptic density.
source: The latter is consistent with our observed decrease in the amplitude of mEPSCs and reduced AMPA-evoked currents and with previous reports of Ntn1 regulating the delivery of GluA1-containing AMPA receptors to the postsynaptic density (Jasmin et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Jasmin et al., 2021 and consistent with current study's findings

claim: Reduced glutamatergic signaling in dopamine neurons largely does not affect appetitive behavior, locomotion, and sensory-motor gating.
source: The general lack of effect of reduced glutamatergic synaptic connectivity on appetitive behavior, locomotion, and sensory-motor gating is consistent with previous observations that reduced glutamatergic signaling in dopamine neurons largely does not affect these behaviors (Zweifel et al., 2009; Hutchison et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Zweifel et al., 2009 and Hutchison et al., 2018

claim: Disrupting GABA neuron function in the VTA induces a hyperdopaminergic phenotype.
source: In contrast, loss of Ntn1 in VTA GABA neurons had a significant effect on multiple behaviors including locomotion, motivation, and acoustic pre-pulse inhibition, all of which are consistent with a hyperdopaminergic phenotype and with previous reports that disrupting GABA neuron function in the VTA induces similar phenotypes (Gore et al., 2017; Soden et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Gore et al., 2017 and Soden et al., 2020

claim: Loss of NMDA receptor signaling in dopamine D1 receptor-expressing neurons prevents the development of amphetamine sensitization.
source: This finding is similar to what has been reported previously in the striatum.(Beutler et al., 2011) , demonstrated that loss of NMDA receptor signaling in dopamine D1 receptor-expressing neurons prevented the development of amphetamine sensitization; however, inactivation of NMDA receptors in D1R and D2R-expressing medium spiny neurons reversed this phenotype (Beutler et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Beutler et al., 2011

claim: Inactivation of NMDA receptors in D1R and D2R-expressing medium spiny neurons reverses the prevention of amphetamine sensitization caused by loss of NMDA receptor signaling in D1R neurons alone.
source: This finding is similar to what has been reported previously in the striatum.(Beutler et al., 2011) , demonstrated that loss of NMDA receptor signaling in dopamine D1 receptor-expressing neurons prevented the development of amphetamine sensitization; however, inactivation of NMDA receptors in D1R and D2R-expressing medium spiny neurons reversed this phenotype (Beutler et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Beutler et al., 2011

claim: Blocking all synaptic transmission from GABA neurons in the VTA results in hyperactivity and increased operant responding.
source: We have previously shown that blocking all synaptic transmission from GABA neurons in the VTA (Gore et al., 2017), or blocking selectively GABA release from VTA GABA neurons (Hutchison et al., 2018) results in hyperactivity and increased operant responding, though to a much greater degree than the effects observed here.
evidence: Cited from Gore et al., 2017

claim: Blocking selectively GABA release from VTA GABA neurons results in hyperactivity and increased operant responding.
source: We have previously shown that blocking all synaptic transmission from GABA neurons in the VTA (Gore et al., 2017), or blocking selectively GABA release from VTA GABA neurons (Hutchison et al., 2018) results in hyperactivity and increased operant responding, though to a much greater degree than the effects observed here.
evidence: Cited from Hutchison et al., 2018

claim: Loss of glutamate signaling in dopamine neurons has only a modest behavioral effect.
source: We and others have also shown that loss of glutamate signaling in dopamine neurons has only a modest behavioral effect (Zweifel et al., 2009; Hutchison et al., 2018) so it is not surprising that reducing mEPSCs onto VTA dopamine neurons has little effect.
evidence: Cited from Zweifel et al., 2009 and Hutchison et al., 2018

claim: Excitatory inputs onto VTA dopamine neurons arise from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus.
source: Simultaneously, excitatory inputs onto VTA dopamine neurons, such as those from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (Soden et al., 2020; Lodge and Grace, 2006), or dorsal raphe nucleus (Qi et al., 2014) would drive the glutamate-dependent burst activation of dopamine neurons (Zweifel et al., 2009; Lodge and Grace, 2006).
evidence: Cited from Soden et al., 2020 and Lodge and Grace, 2006

claim: Excitatory inputs onto VTA dopamine neurons arise from the dorsal raphe nucleus.
source: Simultaneously, excitatory inputs onto VTA dopamine neurons, such as those from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (Soden et al., 2020; Lodge and Grace, 2006), or dorsal raphe nucleus (Qi et al., 2014) would drive the glutamate-dependent burst activation of dopamine neurons (Zweifel et al., 2009; Lodge and Grace, 2006).
evidence: Cited from Qi et al., 2014

claim: Glutamate-dependent burst activation of dopamine neurons is driven by excitatory inputs.
source: Simultaneously, excitatory inputs onto VTA dopamine neurons, such as those from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (Soden et al., 2020; Lodge and Grace, 2006), or dorsal raphe nucleus (Qi et al., 2014) would drive the glutamate-dependent burst activation of dopamine neurons (Zweifel et al., 2009; Lodge and Grace, 2006).
evidence: Cited from Zweifel et al., 2009 and Lodge and Grace, 2006

claim: Suppression of inhibition onto dopamine neurons is a potent means to drive burst activation of these cells.
source: Indeed, inhibitory synaptic connectivity is not altered by the loss of Ntn1, and suppression of inhibition onto dopamine neurons is a potent means to drive the burst activation of these cells (Paladini and Tepper, 1999).
evidence: Cited from Paladini and Tepper, 1999

claim: Excitatory inputs onto GABA neurons within the VTA arise from the lateral habenula.
source: Excitatory inputs onto GABA neurons within the VTA proper, as well as the caudal tail of the VTA, or RMTg, arise from multiple locations including the lateral habenula and ventral pallidum (Omelchenko et al., 2009; Brinschwitz et al., 2010; Tooley et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Omelchenko et al., 2009, Brinschwitz et al., 2010, and Tooley et al., 2018

claim: Excitatory inputs onto GABA neurons within the VTA arise from the ventral pallidum.
source: Excitatory inputs onto GABA neurons within the VTA proper, as well as the caudal tail of the VTA, or RMTg, arise from multiple locations including the lateral habenula and ventral pallidum (Omelchenko et al., 2009; Brinschwitz et al., 2010; Tooley et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Omelchenko et al., 2009, Brinschwitz et al., 2010, and Tooley et al., 2018

claim: Activation of glutamatergic circuits onto VTA GABA neurons is aversive, likely through the activation of GABAergic inputs onto dopamine neurons.
source: Activation of these circuits is aversive, likely through the activation of GABAergic inputs onto dopamine neurons (Tooley et al., 2018; Wulff et al., 2019; Faget et al., 2018; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012).
evidence: Cited from Tooley et al., 2018, Wulff et al., 2019, Faget et al., 2018, and Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012

claim: Ntn1 is a known ligand for Dcc, DSCAM, Neogenin, and Unc5 homologs A-D.
source: Indeed, though Dcc is considered to be its canonical receptor, Ntn1 is a known ligand for several additional receptors, including DSCAM, Neogenin, and Unc5 homologs A-D (Rajasekharan and Kennedy, 2009; Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Rajasekharan and Kennedy, 2009 and Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011

claim: Both Dcc and Unc5c receptors are present in the adult VTA, often in the same cells.
source: Previous work has identified the presence of both Dcc and Unc5c receptors in the adult VTA (often in the same cells) (Manitt et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Manitt et al., 2010

claim: During spinal cord development, Ntn1 expression in the floor plate attracts commissural axons to the midline.
source: It is also interesting to note that during the development of the spinal cord, Ntn1 expression in the floor plate attracts commissural axons to the midline, but following the arrival of these axons at the floor plate, Unc5 expression increases to suppress the attractive actions of DCC signaling (Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011

claim: Following the arrival of commissural axons at the floor plate, Unc5 expression increases to suppress the attractive actions of DCC signaling.
source: It is also interesting to note that during the development of the spinal cord, Ntn1 expression in the floor plate attracts commissural axons to the midline, but following the arrival of these axons at the floor plate, Unc5 expression increases to suppress the attractive actions of DCC signaling (Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011

claim: Slit/Robo signaling repels axons away from the floor plate during development.
source: Of further note, in addition to the role of Ntn1/Dcc/Unc5 signaling in the regulation of commissural axons crossing the midline, Slit/Robo signaling repels axons away from the floor plate (Kidd et al., 1998; Kidd et al., 1999) setting up a push-pull relationship between these pathways.
evidence: Cited from Kidd et al., 1998 and Kidd et al., 1999

claim: Ntn1 is expressed in glial cells in the VTA.
source: Interestingly, (Phillips et al., 2022) also observed the expression of Ntn1 in glial cells.
evidence: Cited from Phillips et al., 2022

claim: VTA GABA neurons project to the nucleus accumbens.
source: However, it is also likely that GABA neurons projecting outside the VTA (for example, to the NAc Brown et al., 2012) are also affected and could contribute to the observed behavioral phenotypes.
evidence: Cited from Brown et al., 2012

claim: Mutations in NTN1 and DCC in humans have been associated with schizophrenia.
source: Mutations in NTN1 (netrin-1) and DCC in humans have been associated with several dopamine-associated psychiatric conditions, including neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia (Wang et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2019; Grant et al., 2012) and major depressive disorder (Tang et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2017; Vosberg et al., 2020; Torres-Berrío et al., 2020), as well as multiple neurodegenerative disorders (Lesnick et al., 2007; Lesnick et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Wang et al., 2018, Tang et al., 2019, and Grant et al., 2012

claim: Mutations in NTN1 and DCC in humans have been associated with major depressive disorder.
source: Mutations in NTN1 (netrin-1) and DCC in humans have been associated with several dopamine-associated psychiatric conditions, including neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia (Wang et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2019; Grant et al., 2012) and major depressive disorder (Tang et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2017; Vosberg et al., 2020; Torres-Berrío et al., 2020), as well as multiple neurodegenerative disorders (Lesnick et al., 2007; Lesnick et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Tang et al., 2019, Zeng et al., 2017, Vosberg et al., 2020, and Torres-Berrío et al., 2020

claim: Mutations in NTN1 and DCC in humans have been associated with multiple neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Mutations in NTN1 (netrin-1) and DCC in humans have been associated with several dopamine-associated psychiatric conditions, including neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia (Wang et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2019; Grant et al., 2012) and major depressive disorder (Tang et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2017; Vosberg et al., 2020; Torres-Berrío et al., 2020), as well as multiple neurodegenerative disorders (Lesnick et al., 2007; Lesnick et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Lesnick et al., 2007, Lesnick et al., 2008, and Lin et al., 2009

claim: A balance of glutamatergic signaling in VTA dopamine and GABA neurons is essential for the normal functioning of the mesolimbic dopamine system.
source: These results suggest that a balance of glutamatergic signaling in these two cell types is essential for the normal functioning of the mesolimbic dopamine system (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of behavioral phenotypes when Ntn1 is knocked out in both cell types simultaneously, as shown in Figure 6A model

claim: Ntn1 regulates the actin cytoskeleton through its activation of the cognate receptor DCC.
source: Likely mechanisms include Ntn1 regulation of the actin cytoskeleton and receptor transport vesicles through its activation of the cognate receptor DCC (Yetnikoff et al., 2010; Rajasekharan and Kennedy, 2009).
evidence: Cited from Yetnikoff et al., 2010 and Rajasekharan and Kennedy, 2009 as a proposed mechanism

claim: Ntn1 regulates receptor transport vesicles through its activation of the cognate receptor DCC.
source: Likely mechanisms include Ntn1 regulation of the actin cytoskeleton and receptor transport vesicles through its activation of the cognate receptor DCC (Yetnikoff et al., 2010; Rajasekharan and Kennedy, 2009).
evidence: Cited from Yetnikoff et al., 2010 and Rajasekharan and Kennedy, 2009 as a proposed mechanism

claim: Netrin's role in modulating excitatory synaptic connectivity is likely confined to postsynaptic mechanisms.
source: Our finding that mEPSC frequency, but not paired-pulse ratio, was affected by Ntn1 loss further suggests netrin's role in modulating excitatory synaptic connectivity is likely confined to postsynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiology data showing changes in mEPSC frequency but not PPR

claim: Reduced excitatory tone on VTA GABA neurons induces behaviors associated with a hyperdopaminergic phenotype.
source: In dopamine neurons, the reduced excitatory tone had a minimal phenotypic behavioral outcome; however, reduced glutamatergic tone on VTA GABA neurons induced behaviors associated with a hyperdopaminergic phenotype.
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings from Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO experiments

claim: Simultaneous loss of Ntn1 function in both VTA dopamine and GABA neurons largely rescues the phenotype observed in GABA-only mutagenesis.
source: Simultaneous loss of Ntn1 function in both cell types largely rescued the phenotype observed in the GABA-only mutagenesis.
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings from DAT-Cre::Vgat-Cre double knockout experiments

claim: Ntn1 loss of function reduces excitatory postsynaptic connectivity in VTA dopamine and GABA neurons.
source: Ntn1 loss-of-function in either cell type resulted in a significant reduction in excitatory postsynaptic connectivity.
evidence: Summary of electrophysiology findings from both DAT-Cre and Vgat-Cre experiments

claim: Reduced excitatory tone on VTA dopamine neurons had minimal phenotypic behavioral outcome.
source: In dopamine neurons, the reduced excitatory tone had a minimal phenotypic behavioral outcome; however, reduced glutamatergic tone on VTA GABA neurons induced behaviors associated with a hyperdopaminergic phenotype.
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings from DAT-Cre Ntn1 cKO experiments

claim: Ntn1 does not regulate inhibitory connectivity in VTA dopamine or GABA neurons.
source: We did not detect significant effects on miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) in VTA dopamine or GABA neurons following Ntn1 mutagenesis in these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting Ntn1 does not play a role in regulating inhibitory connectivity in these cells.
evidence: Inferred from lack of significant effects on mIPSCs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Ntn1 regulates AMPA receptor availability in adult VTA.
source: These results suggest that Ntn1 regulates AMPA receptor availability in adult VTA.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced AMPA-evoked currents but not NMDA-evoked currents following Ntn1 mutagenesis

claim: Loss of excitatory drive onto dopamine neurons can be compensated for through disinhibitory circuits of the VTA.
source: Loss of excitatory drive onto dopamine neurons can likely be compensated for through the many disinhibitory circuits of the VTA.
evidence: Proposed mechanism to explain why DAT-Cre Ntn1 cKO has minimal behavioral effects

claim: Reduced glutamatergic inputs onto VTA GABA neurons would suppress the inhibition of dopamine neurons allowing excitatory drive onto these cells to go unchecked.
source: Thus, reduced glutamatergic inputs onto VTA GABA neurons would suppress the inhibition of dopamine neurons allowing excitatory drive onto these cells to go unchecked, resulting in the phenotypes observed here.
evidence: Proposed mechanism to explain the hyperdopaminergic phenotype in Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice

claim: When excitatory inputs onto dopamine neurons are reduced along with reduced excitatory inputs onto GABA neurons, the combined driving forces of disinhibition and excitation of dopamine neurons are re-equilibrated.
source: When excitatory inputs onto dopamine neurons are also reduced the combined driving forces of disinhibition and excitation of the dopamine neurons are re-equilibrated, restoring balance to the system.
evidence: Proposed mechanism to explain the rescue of phenotypes in double knockout mice

claim: There is a push-pull relationship between netrin/Dcc/Unc5 and Slit/Robo signaling pathways in which netrin/Dcc/Unc5 regulates excitation and Slit/Robo signaling regulates inhibition.
source: We previously demonstrated that Robo2 maintains inhibitory synaptic connectivity in the adult VTA (Gore et al., 2017), suggesting the existence of another 'push/pull' relationship between these two pathways in which netrin/Dcc/Unc5 regulates excitation and Slit/Robo signaling regulates inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the current findings on Ntn1 regulating excitation and prior work on Robo2 regulating inhibition (Gore et al., 2017)

claim: The remaining Ntn1 expressing cells that do not co-localize with Th or Slc32a1 are likely glutamatergic neurons or possibly glial cells.
source: The remaining Ntn1 expressing cells that do not co-localize with Th or Slc32a1 are likely glutamatergic neurons (Morales and Margolis, 2017), or possibly glial cells (Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred from the cell type composition of the VTA and cited from Morales and Margolis, 2017 and Phillips et al., 2022

claim: Ntn1 loss of function does not result in non-cell autonomous effects on mEPSCs from non-targeted cells.
source: To address this, we recorded mEPSCs from non-YFP-expressing (presumptively non-dopamine) neurons in DAT-Cre mice injected with Ntn1 CRISPR or control virus, and from non-YFP-expressing (presumptively non-GABA) neurons in Vgat-Cre injected mice. We did not observe significant non-cell autonomous effects on mEPSCs from non-targeted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Electrophysiology data from non-targeted cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 loss of function does not result in non-cell autonomous effects on mIPSCs from non-targeted cells.
source: Similarly, we also did not observe non-cell autonomous effects on mIPSCs from non-targeted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Electrophysiology data from non-targeted cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with no statistical significance

claim: Ntn1 loss of function in VTA dopamine neurons does not significantly affect locomotor differences in the open field arena.
source: There were no significant locomotor differences associated with the loss of Ntn1 function in the open field arena (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Open field locomotor data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with no statistical significance

claim: Pre-calorie restriction body weights in Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice do not differ from controls.
source: In contrast to DAT-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice, pre-calorie restriction body weights in Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice did not differ from controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Body weight data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with no statistical significance

claim: Vgat-Cre Ntn1 cKO mice show increased distance traveled during the open field test relative to controls.
source: The lack of observed significance in the time in center in the context of increased edge time may reflect the hyperactivity observed following Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA GABA neurons, consistent with this possibility, we did observe increased distance traveled during the open field test in these mice relative to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Open field locomotor data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance (p<0.05)

claim: Pre-calorie restriction body weights in DAT-Cre::Vgat-Cre double knockout mice do not differ from controls.
source: Similarly, loss of Ntn1 in both VTA GABA and dopamine neurons resulted in operant responding during FR1 and FR5 that was similar to controls (Figure 6D) and pre-calorie restriction body weights did not differ between the groups.
evidence: Body weight data mentioned in text, presumably shown in supplementary figure

claim: DAT-Cre::Vgat-Cre double knockout mice show a modest increase in daytime locomotion.
source: Simultaneous Ntn1 loss of function in VTA GABA and dopamine neurons largely reversed the hyperlocomotor phenotype (Figure 6C) observed with Ntn1 mutagenesis in VTA GABA neurons alone, though a modest, increase in daytime locomotion remained (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Locomotor activity data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance for daytime activity (p<0.05)

claim: No sex differences were observed in any of the behavioral or electrophysiological results.
source: No sex differences were observed in any of the behavioral or electrophysiological results.
evidence: Statement in Methods section indicating post-hoc analysis found no sex differences

claim: Thigmotaxis (increased time on edge) has been validated as a measure of anxiogenic behavior.
source: Thigmotaxis, the tendency of mice to remain in close proximity to the walls of an enclosure, has been validated as a measure of anxiogenic behavior (Simon et al., 1994; Seibenhener and Wooten, 2015), with increased time on edge signifying increased anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: Cited from Simon et al., 1994 and Seibenhener and Wooten, 2015
